3070:
When something is commemorative, it means it was made, designed, or done specifically to honor and keep alive the memory of an important person, event, or moment from the past.

The key idea is intentional remembering — the thing exists for the purpose of making sure people don't forget something that mattered.

Imagine a great leader passed away fifty years ago. People still feel that their life and work deserve to be remembered. So they create a special coin with that leader's face on it. That coin is commemorative — it was made to commemorate (honor the memory of) that leader.

The word always answers the question: Why does this thing exist? And the answer is always: To honor and preserve a memory.
What kinds of things can be commemorative?

Almost any object, event, or gesture can be commemorative, as long as its purpose is to honor a memory:

  • A commemorative stamp — a postage stamp printed to mark a historic event or person
  • A commemorative coin or medal — a special-edition coin released to mark an anniversary or honor someone
  • A commemorative plaque — a metal or stone plate fixed to a wall, reminding people of what happened there
  • A commemorative ceremony — a formal gathering held to honor a past event (like a battle, a tragedy, or a founding)
  • A commemorative edition — a special reprinting of a book, often with extra content, released on a significant anniversary
  • A commemorative march — a walk organized to honor those who suffered or died for a cause
  • A commemorative speech — words spoken in tribute to someone or something important

Commemorative things are almost always formal and serious in purpose, even if the event being remembered was joyful (like a nation's independence). There is a feeling of respect and duty to remember built into the word.

It can apply to both happy and sad occasions:

  • A commemorative concert for a beloved musician who passed away → sad
  • A commemorative parade marking 100 years of a country's independence → proud and celebratory

In both cases, the purpose is the same: to ensure the memory lives on.

Commemorative does not just mean "old" or "historical." A dusty old photo is not automatically commemorative. It becomes commemorative only when someone has deliberately used it or created it to honor a memory.

Also, something commemorative is not the same as something merely popular or decorative. A mug with a city's skyline on it is decorative. But a mug released specifically to mark the 50th anniversary of that city's founding? That's commemorative.
How it differs from similar words

Memorial — closely related, but "memorial" most often refers to something honoring people who have died, especially in war or tragedy. A memorial is built for loss. Commemorative is broader — it can honor living milestones too, like anniversaries and achievements. (A memorial wall. A commemorative stamp for a sports victory.)

Celebratory — this word is purely about joy and festivity. Commemorative carries more weight and seriousness, even when the occasion is positive.

Historic — something is historic because it was important. Something is commemorative because someone is actively choosing to honor that importance now.
A sentence to tie it all together

The government released a commemorative coin on the 75th anniversary of the country's independence, so that citizens would always remember the sacrifices made for their freedom.

Here, "commemorative" tells you instantly: this coin was created on purpose, to honor a memory, because that memory matters.
Commemorative = made or done to honor and preserve the memory of something important from the past.
3071:
To commence means to begin or to start something. That's it at the heart of it. When something commences, it moves from a state of not yet happening into a state of actively happening.

A ceremony commences. A trial commences. Construction commences. In each case, the thing goes from "not started" to "now underway."

This is the most important thing to understand about "commence" — it is not just a fancy synonym for "start." The three words overlap in meaning, but they carry different weight and feel.

Start is casual and everyday. You start your car. You start a conversation with a friend. It's the word you'd use without thinking twice.

Begin is neutral. It works in both everyday and slightly formal situations. You begin reading a book. A story begins with "Once upon a time."

Commence is formal and official. It belongs in courtrooms, ceremonies, military operations, legal documents, academic settings, and official announcements. If you used "commence" when talking to a friend about making a sandwich, it would sound strange and overly stiff — almost like you're mocking a general giving orders.

So the rule of thumb is: the more official, structured, or serious the situation, the more natural "commence" sounds.

"Commence" is flexible. Here are the main ways it works:

1. With no object (intransitive) — something simply begins on its own:

  • "The ceremony will commence at noon."
  • "The trial commenced on Monday."

Here, nothing directly follows "commence" — the subject itself is what begins.

2. With a direct object (transitive) — someone starts something:

  • "The judge commenced the proceedings."
  • "They commenced construction of the new highway."

Here, there is something being started — a proceedings, a construction — and "commence" acts on it.

3. Commence + -ing verb (gerund):

  • "The workers commenced drilling into the ground."
  • "She commenced writing her report."

This pattern is very common. You commence doing something.

4. Commence + "to" + base verb (infinitive):

  • "The soldiers commenced to fire."
  • "He commenced to read the charges aloud."

This is less common than the -ing pattern, but it is grammatically correct and you will encounter it.

5. Commence with + noun:

  • "We will commence with the opening remarks."
  • "The session commenced with a minute of silence."

This is used when specifying what specifically the beginning consists of.

One subtle but important quality of "commence" is that it almost always implies a deliberate, planned, or official beginning — not something accidental or casual. Things that "commence" tend to be events or processes that were anticipated, scheduled, or formally set in motion.

A fire starts (it just happens). But military fire commences (it is ordered). A party starts. But a state funeral commences.

This is why you'll almost always see "commence" attached to structured, institutional events: legal proceedings, academic programs, military actions, construction projects, formal meetings, and ceremonies.

Certain words pair with "commence" very naturally in formal writing and speech:

  • Commence operations — used in military and business contexts
  • Commence proceedings — used in law
  • Commence construction / work — used in project management and engineering
  • Commence firing — used in military contexts
  • Commence trading — used in finance (when a stock begins being traded)
  • Commence negotiations — used in diplomacy and business

The noun form of "commence" is commencement. While it generally means "the beginning of something," it has a very specific and widely recognized use in American English: a commencement ceremony is a graduation ceremony — the official beginning of a graduate's new chapter in life after completing their studies. You may hear "commencement speech" or "commencement day" in this context.
A Quick Reality Check on Usage

"Commence" is not a word you need to use in daily conversation. Native speakers rarely do. But you absolutely will encounter it — in legal documents, in formal announcements, in literature, in historical texts, in news reporting, and in official communications. Understanding it deeply means you'll never be confused when you see it, and you'll know exactly when it's appropriate to use it yourself.

When in doubt, ask: "Is this situation formal, official, or structured?" If yes, "commence" fits naturally. If not, "start" or "begin" is the better choice.
3072: To commend someone means to praise them sincerely, express formal approval of them, or recommend them to others as being worthy. It is more than just saying "good job" — when you commend someone, you are putting your own credibility behind them. You are saying, in effect: I vouch for this person or thing.

1. To praise or express formal, weighty approval

This is the most common use. You commend someone when you acknowledge their good work, behavior, or qualities — often in a way that carries a tone of ceremony or official recognition.

  • A general commends a soldier for bravery in battle.
  • A teacher commends a student in front of the whole class.
  • A manager commends an employee at the end of a difficult project.

The person doing the commending often has some authority or standing, but that is not a strict rule. What matters is the tone: commending feels deliberate, sincere, and dignified. It is not how a friend casually raves about a movie — it is the tone you would find in an award ceremony speech, a formal letter, or a heartfelt public acknowledgment.

2. To recommend something as worthy of attention or use

You can also commend a thing — a book, an idea, a plan, a course of action — to someone. Here it means: "I believe this is good, and I want you to seriously consider it."

  • "I commend this novel to anyone who loves history."
  • "The committee commended the proposal as a sound approach."

In everyday conversation, people often say recommend instead, but commend carries a warmer, more personal endorsement. You are not just pointing something out — you are standing behind it.

3. To entrust someone or something to another's care (formal / literary)

This is an older, more literary sense. To commend someone to the care of another means to formally place them in that person's protection or responsibility.

  • "She commended her children to the care of her sister before departing."
  • "He commended his soul to God." (a phrase common in prayers and at death)
  • "I commend this matter entirely to your judgment." (= I trust you to handle this)

You will encounter this sense in literature, religious writing, and formal speeches. In modern everyday speech, people would more likely say entrust or leave in the care of — but recognizing this use will help you when you read older texts or formal writing.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Commend sits in the middle ground between warm and formal. It does not feel gushing or over-the-top — it feels measured, sincere, and substantial. When someone says "I commend your courage," it lands with more gravity and permanence than "You were so brave!" It is the word of speeches, recommendation letters, official recognitions, and serious, heartfelt moments.

Understanding how commend differs from similar words is often what cements the meaning permanently:

  • Praise — more general and used in any setting, formal or casual. Commend is more deliberate and implies a degree of endorsement or recommendation, not just approval.
  • Recommend — also about suggesting something as good. But recommend tends to be practical ("I recommend this mechanic"), while commend carries greater emotional or moral weight ("I commend this doctor's selfless dedication").
  • Applaud — to approve of or celebrate, often with enthusiasm. More expressive and emotionally charged than the measured tone of commend.
  • Endorse — to officially support or approve something. Close to commend in formal contexts, but endorse is more common in commercial or political settings (endorsing a product, a candidate).

Getting familiar with how a word is used grammatically is just as important as knowing what it means:

  • Commend someone for something:
    "The principal commended the students for their honesty."*
  • Commend something to someone:
    "I commend this approach to your attention."*
  • Commend someone to someone's care:
    "He commended his elderly mother to the care of his brother."*
  • Something commends itself to someone:
    "The simplicity of the plan commended itself to the committee."*

That last pattern deserves special attention. When something "commends itself" to someone, it means the thing made a positive impression on its own merits — it appealed to them or seemed the right choice. Nothing is actively doing the recommending; the thing's own qualities do the work. It is an elegant, slightly literary construction you will come across in formal writing.

Across all three meanings, there is one thread that connects them:

You are placing something or someone in a position of value or trust — either in other people's minds (by praising or recommending), or in another person's hands (by entrusting).

Whether you are commending a colleague's work in a meeting, commending a book to a friend, or commending a child to a guardian's care, you are actively vouching for the worth or safety of something you value.
3073:
When something is commendable, it means it deserves praise and positive recognition. It tells you that a person's action, effort, quality, or behavior is good enough — and noticeable enough — to be acknowledged and appreciated by others.

Think of it this way: not everything good gets noticed or recognized. But when something is commendable, it stands out in a positive way. It clears a bar that makes people say, "That's worth praising."

Imagine a student who has been struggling with math all year. One day, instead of giving up, she stays after school every single day, works extra hard, and improves her grade significantly. Her teacher might say:

"Your dedication is commendable."

The teacher isn't saying she's a genius. She's saying: "What you did is worthy of praise. It's the kind of thing people should be recognized for."

That's exactly what commendable means — worthy of praise.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

This is important to understand, because how a word feels is just as important as what it means.

Commendable is:

  • Formal and measured. It's not a word you'd casually say to a friend. It carries a dignified, respectful tone — like something a teacher, manager, judge, or senior person would say.
  • Warm but controlled. It's not over-the-top like "incredible" or "amazing." It's a calm, sincere form of praise — the kind that feels serious and genuine.
  • Objective-sounding. It suggests that the praise isn't just a personal opinion — it implies that most reasonable people would agree the thing deserves recognition.

Almost anything a person does, shows, or stands for can be called commendable — as long as it earns positive recognition. Here are the main categories:

1. Efforts and actions

"His effort to rebuild his community after the flood was commendable."
"She made a commendable attempt to resolve the conflict peacefully."

2. Personal qualities and character traits

"His honesty in a world full of dishonesty is truly commendable."
"Her patience with difficult students is commendable."

3. Behavior and conduct

"The soldiers showed commendable discipline under pressure."
"The company's commendable behavior during the crisis earned public trust."

4. Achievements and performances

"It was a commendable performance, even if it wasn't perfect."
"He delivered a commendable speech for someone with no experience."

This is a subtle but very useful thing to understand.

Commendable sits in the middle of the praise scale — above simply "good" or "decent," but below "exceptional," "outstanding," or "extraordinary."

Think of it like this:

Okay → Good → Commendable → Excellent → Outstanding → Extraordinary

So when you say something is commendable, you're saying it's clearly praiseworthy and deserving of recognition — but you're not necessarily saying it's the best thing ever or absolutely perfect. It's honest, solid, meaningful praise.

For example:

"It was a commendable effort" — This means the effort was real and deserves praise, but it might not have been a flawless or record-breaking achievement.

This makes commendable a very honest and respectful word. It doesn't over-inflate the praise.
A Very Common and Useful Pattern

One of the most common ways you'll see this word used is in this construction:

"It is commendable that..."

This structure lets you praise a fact or situation, not just a person.

"It is commendable that the government decided to listen to the people."
"It is commendable that he admitted his mistake so openly."

Understanding the opposite helps sharpen the meaning.

If something is not commendable, it might be:

  • Blameworthy — deserving criticism, not praise.
  • Disgraceful — something that brings shame.
  • Deplorable — something deeply bad and upsetting.
  • Reprehensible — something morally wrong that people strongly disapprove of.

These are the opposites of commendable. Where commendable earns you recognition and respect, these words earn you condemnation.

These words are close in meaning to commendable and can help you understand it better by comparison:

  • Praiseworthy — Perhaps the most direct synonym. Literally means "worthy of praise." Almost identical in meaning, slightly more everyday.
  • Admirable — Something that makes people feel admiration. Very close in meaning but slightly warmer in tone.
  • Laudable — Very formal; means the same thing but used in more academic or official contexts.
  • Meritorious — Means having merit or strong qualities that deserve recognition. More formal and often used in official or military contexts.

The difference between these words and commendable is often just tone and context — commendable strikes a perfect balance between being formal and still being natural in everyday writing or speech.

What it meansDeserving of praise and positive recognition
ToneFormal, respectful, sincere, measured
Strength of praiseSolid and clear — above "good," but not "extraordinary"
Used forEfforts, actions, qualities, behavior, achievements
Feeling it givesHonest, dignified approval — like a nod of genuine respect
One Final Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word commendable, just ask yourself:

"Is this something that deserves a genuine, respectful nod of praise?"

If the answer is yes — that's commendable. It's the word you use when something is good in a way that's real, visible, and worth saying out loud.
3074:
A commendation is an act of formal, public praise given to someone because they did something exceptionally well, went beyond what was expected of them, or showed outstanding qualities like bravery, skill, or dedication. It is not ordinary, everyday praise like saying "good job" to a friend. It carries weight, officialness, and significance. It says: "What you did was truly noteworthy, and the world should know it."

Think of it this way — if your teacher tells you privately that your essay was great, that is a compliment. But if your school principal announces your name in an assembly and gives you a framed certificate for the best essay of the year, that is a commendation.

The word carries two senses that are deeply connected to each other:

The first sense is the act of commending — meaning the act of formally praising or recognising someone. For example: "The commendation of the officer took place at a ceremony held by the mayor." Here, commendation refers to the event or the act of formally praising that person.

The second sense is the object or award that results from that act — a physical certificate, a medal, a formal letter, or an official written statement that records the praise. For example: "The firefighter received a commendation for rescuing three people from a burning building." Here, commendation refers to the award or recognition itself that was handed to the firefighter.

In everyday use, you will encounter both senses freely, and context will always make it clear which one is meant.

Commendations are typically given by a person or body in authority — a government, a military organisation, a school, a company, a police department, or any institution that has the standing to officially recognise people. This is important because it is the authority and formality of the source that gives a commendation its power and meaning.

Common situations where commendations are given include:

A soldier who showed exceptional bravery under enemy fire might receive a military commendation. A police officer who solved a complex case or protected civilians at great personal risk might receive a commendation for service. A student who achieved the highest marks in a national exam might receive a commendation for academic excellence. An employee who saved the company through extraordinary dedication might receive a letter of commendation from the CEO.

In every case, the message is the same: your actions were so outstanding that they deserve to be formally acknowledged and remembered.

While commendation leans formal, it exists on a spectrum. At its most formal extreme, it is an official military decoration or a government award. Slightly less formal but still very serious, it is a letter of commendation from a manager or a school award. It can also be used in speech and writing to describe strong, genuine, heartfelt praise, even without a physical award. For example: "The judge's commendation of the young architect's design moved everyone in the room."

What never changes, regardless of where it sits on this spectrum, is the sense of genuine, weighty, meaningful recognition — it is never casual or trivial.
How It Relates to Other Forms of the Same Word

Understanding the family of words it belongs to will make the meaning even clearer and help you use them all correctly.

The verb is commend, meaning to formally praise someone or to recommend them strongly. "The general commended the soldier for her courage."

The adjective is commendable, meaning worthy of praise. "Her dedication to the project was truly commendable."

The noun is commendation, the act or result of commending. "She received a commendation at the annual awards ceremony."

Notice how all three words share the same root idea: something deserves to be praised, and that praise is being expressed in a meaningful, sincere, often formal way.

Knowing related words will help you understand commendation more precisely by seeing where it fits among its neighbours.

A tribute is praise offered to honour someone, often in an emotional or memorial context. A citation is very close in meaning to commendation and is often used in military or academic contexts specifically for a written official statement of praise. An accolade is a strong mark of recognition or approval, often less formal. Praise is the broad, general word for expressing that something is good. Recognition is the acknowledgement that someone's efforts or achievements are valued.

Among all of these, commendation is distinctly formal and carries a sense of institutional authority behind it.

In natural English, commendation is most often seen with certain words:

You receive or earn a commendation. You give, issue, or award a commendation. You deserve a commendation. It can be a letter of commendation, a certificate of commendation, or a military commendation. You might receive high commendation for something that nearly won an award but didn't quite get first place — this is common in competitions and shows that the work was deeply appreciated even if it didn't win.
A Few Sentences to See It in Action

"The young nurse received a commendation from the hospital board for her tireless work during the crisis."

"The army general's commendation of the battalion raised the morale of every soldier present."

"At the end of the year, several students earned commendations for their contributions to the school community."

"His painting received a high commendation at the national art competition — it didn't win first prize, but the judges made clear it was extraordinary."

"She framed the letter of commendation from her director and hung it on her office wall."

If you want to truly feel the word, not just know it intellectually — a commendation is the moment when an institution looks at an individual and says: "You did not have to do what you did. You went further than required. You made a difference. And we want everyone to know it." It is respectful, admiring, and carries genuine weight. It elevates a person. It marks a moment as worth remembering.

That is commendation — not just praise, but praise that counts.
3075:
"Commensurate" describes a relationship between two things where one is at exactly the right level or degree in proportion to the other. When two things are commensurate, they are balanced and appropriately matched. Neither is too large nor too small relative to the other. They fit together the way they should.

The word almost always appears with the preposition "with," forming the phrase "commensurate with."
A concrete example to lock it in

Imagine you are applying for a job and the posting says: "Salary commensurate with experience." This means the salary will be proportionally appropriate to your level of experience. If you have ten years of experience, you will be offered a high salary. If you have two years, a lower one. The salary will reflect — will match, will be in the right proportion to — however much experience you bring to the table. The two things are in balance with each other.
The crucial distinction: "commensurate" is not the same as "equal"

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

"Equal" means the same amount. "Commensurate" means proportionally appropriate. These are different ideas.

Consider two employees at the same company. One is a senior engineer earning $150,000. The other is a junior engineer earning $70,000. Both salaries can be described as "commensurate with their experience" — even though the numbers are completely different — because each salary is at the right level for the experience that person brings. Commensurate is about the relationship between two things, not about them being identical.

Think of it like a well-calibrated scale. When things are commensurate, the scale is perfectly balanced. The weight on one side corresponds correctly to the weight on the other. When things are not commensurate, the scale tips — something is too heavy or too light relative to the other side.

Consider the sentence: "The punishment should be commensurate with the crime." A minor offence deserves a mild punishment; a serious crime deserves a severe one. The punishment should be calibrated to the gravity of the crime — neither too harsh for something small, nor too lenient for something major. That proportional fit is exactly what "commensurate" captures.

Or: "The risks were not commensurate with the rewards." Here, the scale is tipped. The rewards are too small (or the risks too large) for the situation to feel balanced or fair. Something is out of proportion.

Or: "She was given a level of responsibility commensurate with her abilities." She wasn't overwhelmed with more than she could handle, nor was she under-used with tasks far below her capability. What she was given matched what she was capable of.

Notice something across all these examples: when things are commensurate, there is a feeling of rightness and fairness. The word carries a moral undertone of justice and appropriate balance. When a punishment fits a crime, when a reward matches an effort, when a salary reflects an experience level — we feel that things are as they should be. This is why "commensurate" is very common in legal writing, employment contracts, policy discussions, and ethical arguments — anywhere people are talking about what is appropriate, fair, or properly proportioned.
What it looks like when things are NOT commensurate

The opposite of commensurate is disproportionate. The formal antonym is incommensurate. If a thief steals a loaf of bread and is sentenced to twenty years in prison, the punishment is not commensurate with the crime — it is wildly disproportionate. If someone works exhausting 80-hour weeks but earns minimum wage, their compensation is not commensurate with their effort. The scale, in each case, is badly tipped.
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: commensurate means proportionally appropriate to something else — matched to it in the right degree, neither too much nor too little.
3076: A comment is a remark or observation that someone makes about something — a person, a situation, an idea, an event, or a piece of work. The most important thing to understand about a comment is that it is secondary: it always reacts to, responds to, or reflects on something that already exists. You don't make a comment out of nowhere; there's always something being commented on.

Imagine your friend shows you a new jacket. You say, "The color suits you." That's a comment — a brief, focused thing you said about something in front of you.

Comments can be:

  • Positive: "She made a kind comment about his presentation."
  • Negative: "He passed a rude comment about her work."
  • Neutral: "She made a comment that the train was running late."

The word "comment" itself carries no emotional charge. It doesn't tell you whether the remark was nice or nasty — that depends entirely on what the comment said. The word is just the container.

When politicians, executives, or celebrities speak to journalists, their words are often called comments. "The minister made no comment on the allegations." "The company declined to comment."

The famous phrase "no comment" means the person is refusing to say anything at all — usually because the topic is legally sensitive or they don't want their words used against them. It is a deliberate, formal silence.

A comment can also be a written note added to a document or text — not part of the main writing, but attached to it in order to explain, question, or give feedback on a part of it.

When a teacher reads your essay and writes "needs more evidence here" in the margin, that's a comment. When a colleague reviewing your report highlights a paragraph and adds a note asking for clarification, that's a comment too.

In digital tools — Google Docs, Microsoft Word, PDF readers — the "comment" feature works exactly this way: you select a piece of text, attach a note to it, and that note floats beside the main document, visible to others but separate from the actual content.

One of the most familiar modern uses is the comment section — the area below a YouTube video, a news article, a social media post, or a blog, where anyone can write their response or reaction. Each individual post in that area is called a comment.

"She left a comment under the video." "The comments on that post were divided." "He turned off comments on his photo."

This is a natural extension of the original meaning: someone has posted something; you are responding to it. Your response is a comment.

This is a completely separate but very important meaning. In programming, a comment is a piece of text written inside the code that the computer completely ignores when it runs the program. It exists only for human readers — to explain what the code does, why a decision was made, or to leave notes for other programmers who might read the code later.

For example:

```
// This calculates the total price including tax
calculateTotal(items)
```

The first line (starting with //) is a comment. The computer skips over it entirely. Only the actual instruction runs. Comments in code are therefore invisible to the machine but essential for human understanding.

This meaning is precise and technical: a comment in code is a human-readable note embedded in source code, invisible to the executing machine.
The figurative use: "a comment on something"

In a more abstract, literary sense, something can be a comment on something else — even without words being spoken. This means it reflects, reveals, or says something meaningful about a subject.

"The novel is a sharp comment on the loneliness of modern city life." — The novel, through its story, is making a statement about something in the real world.

"His extravagant spending was a comment on how little he valued hard work." — His behavior is communicating something, even without words.

"The fact that no one attended was itself a comment on how unpopular the policy was." — An absence, a silence, or an action can "comment" on a situation by revealing the truth about it.

This figurative use is more common in writing, journalism, and criticism than in ordinary conversation.
How it differs from similar words

These words are close to "comment" but not identical:

  • Remark: Nearly identical to "comment" in most situations — you can often swap them. If there's any difference at all, a remark tends to feel slightly more spontaneous and off-the-cuff, while a comment can feel slightly more considered. But in practice, they are used interchangeably most of the time.
  • Statement: More formal, more deliberate, and more official than a comment. A statement is usually longer, more structured, and carries more weight. A press release contains "a statement"; a quick reaction to something is "a comment."
  • Opinion: Your opinion is your overall view or position on something. A comment is a specific, concrete instance of expressing something — one thing you said or wrote. Your opinion can remain unexpressed; a comment, by definition, has been said or written.
  • Observation: A comment that specifically points out something you have noticed. All observations are comments, but not all comments are observations — a comment could be a reaction, a question, or a judgment, not just a noticing.
  • Criticism: A comment that expresses a negative judgment about something. All criticism is a comment, but not all comments are criticism. A comment is neutral — criticism is specifically negative.
  • Annotation: A written comment added to a text — usually to explain, analyze, or question it. An annotation is a type of comment, but the word "annotation" is more formal and specifically refers to written notes on written material (books, documents, manuscripts).

• "Make a comment" — to say or write something about a topic. The most standard way to use the noun.
  • "No comment" — a refusal to speak on a subject, especially in formal or public settings.
  • "Pass comment" — (more common in British English) to offer a remark or opinion, often unsolicited.
  • "An offhand comment" — a casual, unplanned remark, sometimes unintentionally hurtful because it wasn't thought through.
  • "An off-the-cuff comment" — something said quickly and spontaneously, without prior preparation.
  • "The comment section" — the area of a website where readers post their responses.
  • "A comment on [something]" — a remark, action, or work that reveals or reflects something about a subject (the figurative use).
  • "Comments are welcome" — an invitation for people to share their responses or feedback.
  • "Without comment" — doing something or reporting something without offering any opinion or reaction to it.
The essential idea, in one place

A comment is always supplementary — it adds to, responds to, or reflects on something that already exists. Whether it's a quick remark in conversation, a note added to a document, a reply posted under an article, or a line of text in computer code that the machine ignores — in every case, the comment is not the main thing. It is something said, written, or implied about the main thing.

That secondary, responsive quality is the thread that connects every use of this word.
3077:
When you comment, you say or write something that expresses your thoughts, observations, or opinion about something. The key idea is that there is already something in front of you — an event, a situation, a piece of work, someone's behaviour, a statement — and you are reacting to it from your own perspective.

Think of it this way: a reporter asks a politician about a scandal. The politician either comments (says something about it) or refuses to comment (stays silent). In both cases, the scandal came first, and the politician's reaction to it is the comment.

A few things are quietly embedded in this word that make it precise:

You are responding to something that already exists. You don't comment into thin air. There is always a subject — something you are commenting on or about. A painting, a decision, a person's behaviour, a news story — something is there, and you are reacting to it.

You are speaking as an observer or evaluator. When you comment, you are not the main actor in the situation. You are on the outside, looking in and sharing your view. A food critic comments on a dish; a teacher comments on a student's essay; a friend comments on your new haircut. In all cases, they are observing something and offering a perspective.

"To comment" is neutral. This is very important. The word itself carries no positive or negative charge. You can make a kind comment, a harsh comment, a brief comment, or a thoughtful comment. The word simply describes the act of sharing a reaction — the tone of that reaction comes from context, not from the word itself. This is what separates it from words like criticise (which is always negative) or praise (which is always positive).

There are three main structures you will see:

1. Comment + on + something (most common)
This is the standard form. The word "on" is almost always the natural preposition after "comment."

"She commented on his choice of words."
"The minister refused to comment on the investigation."
"He commented on how much she had changed."

2. Comment + that + a full statement
When you want to report what someone said, you use "that" followed by their full thought.

"She commented that the presentation was unclear."
"He commented that the city had grown a lot since his last visit."
"They commented that the food was better than expected."

3. Comment (alone, with no object)
Sometimes "comment" stands on its own, without naming what it is about — especially when the subject is already understood.

"He chose not to comment."
"When asked about the incident, she simply didn't comment."
"The company declined to comment."
Contexts Where You'll Encounter This Verb

In everyday speech and writing, this is the most common use. People comment on news articles, on each other's choices, on films, on a friend's Instagram post, on a sporting result.

"Dozens of people commented on her video."
"He commented under the photo with a laughing emoji."
"Everyone was commenting on how well she spoke."

In formal and professional settings, the word takes on a slightly more considered tone — experts, officials, and analysts "comment" on events, policies, and reports.

"The professor commented briefly on the student's methodology."
"Several economists commented on the government's decision."
"She was asked to comment on the findings."

In programming and coding, "to comment" has a specialised technical meaning: to add explanatory text inside code that the computer ignores, or to temporarily disable a line of code. This is called "commenting out" code.

"I commented out that section to test the rest of the program."
"Make sure to comment your code so others can understand it."
"She commented the function with a short description of what it does."

This meaning is entirely separate from the general meaning — if you're not a programmer, you may never use it this way. But it's worth knowing it exists.

This deserves its own mention because it's so widely used. "No comment" is a fixed phrase — said exactly as those two words — meaning: I am refusing to say anything about this. It's used by people in legal trouble, by politicians under fire, or by anyone who doesn't want to be quoted on a sensitive matter.

"When asked about the allegations, the CEO said, 'No comment.'"

It carries the feeling of deliberate silence — not not knowing, but choosing not to speak.
How "To Comment" Differs from Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but are not identical:

Remark — Nearly the same as comment, but a remark tends to be more spontaneous, almost thrown out casually. A comment can be more considered and deliberate. You remark on something in passing; you comment on it with a bit more intention — though this distinction is subtle and not always observed strictly.

Observe — More formal than comment. When you "observe" something in conversation, you are making a careful, often measured point. It sounds more thoughtful and academic.

"She observed that the data showed a clear pattern." (careful, analytical)
"She commented that the data was interesting." (more relaxed, conversational)

Note — To "note" something is to point it out, often in a careful, factual way. It draws attention to a specific detail rather than offering a full reaction.

Criticise — Always negative. You criticise only when you're pointing out faults or failures.

Annotate — To write explanatory notes directly onto or alongside a text. More specific and physical than "comment."

Review — A more formal, structured, and comprehensive evaluation, usually of a creative work or a process.

"To comment" is comfortable in both. It doesn't feel out of place in a newspaper article, in a legal deposition, in academic writing, or in casual conversation with a friend. Few words travel so smoothly across registers.
A Few More Examples to See It in Action

"She was hesitant to comment on the ongoing trial."
"He commented quietly that the concert wasn't what he'd expected."
"Feel free to comment on the draft and suggest changes."
"Nobody commented on how late he had arrived."
"The spokesperson commented that the company remained committed to transparency."
"Don't comment on things you don't understand."
"He commented favourably on her work ethic."

To comment is to offer a spoken or written reaction — an opinion, observation, or thought — about something that is already in front of you. It is a neutral act: neither inherently kind nor harsh, neither formal nor informal. It simply means: here is something, and here is what I think about it. The word's precision lies in that sense of responding to something, from the outside, as an observer with a perspective to share.
3078:
A commentary is a piece of spoken or written content in which someone explains, describes, or shares their thoughts and opinions about something else — an event, a text, a situation, a work of art, or anything happening in the world. The single most important thing to understand about the word is this: a commentary always has a subject. It exists to respond to, explain, or reflect on something outside itself.

Think of it this way: a cricket match happens on the field. The commentator in the booth speaks continuously about that match — describing what's happening, explaining why it matters, offering opinions. That stream of speech is the commentary. The match is the subject; the commentary is the layer on top of it.
The two broad flavors of commentary

Commentary generally does one of two things — or both at once.

The first is explanation. Here, the purpose is to help someone understand something. A scholar might write a commentary on an ancient religious text, going through it passage by passage and explaining what each section means, what historical context surrounds it, what the author likely intended. The reader of the text might find it confusing or dense; the commentary is there to make it clearer. Biblical commentaries, for instance, have been written for centuries to help ordinary readers understand scripture more deeply.

The second is opinion and analysis. Here, the purpose is to share a viewpoint, evaluate, or reflect. A journalist writes commentary on a political decision, not just reporting what happened, but explaining what it means, why it matters, and what they think of it. A film critic's commentary on a movie doesn't just describe the plot — it interprets the director's choices, judges the performances, and places the film in a broader cultural context.

In practice, most commentaries blend both. A good sports commentator, for example, describes what's happening (explanation) while also offering judgments about a player's technique or a team's strategy (opinion).
Commentary across different areas of life

You'll encounter this word in many different settings, and it's helpful to see how it works in each one.

In sports, commentary is the live, spoken, real-time description of what's unfolding during a match or game. The person doing it is called a commentator. The commentary flows continuously as events happen — it's dynamic and immediate. The phrase "running commentary" comes from this sense. A "running commentary" means an ongoing, moment-by-moment description of something as it happens, whether it's a football match, a surgical procedure being described for medical students, or someone narrating their own thought process aloud.

In journalism and politics, commentary refers to opinion pieces — writing or speech that goes beyond reporting facts and expresses a view, makes an argument, or analyzes the significance of events. When a newspaper labels something "commentary" or "opinion," it's signaling: this is not neutral reporting. This is a writer's informed perspective. Political commentary, social commentary, cultural commentary — these all refer to observations and reflections on what's happening in society, offered by someone who has thought carefully about it.

In literature and academia, a commentary is a detailed explanatory work written about another text. A student might write a commentary on a poem, going stanza by stanza and explaining the imagery, the themes, and the language choices. A legal commentary explains and interprets the meaning of laws or court judgments. A philosophical commentary unpacks a dense text by a thinker like Kant or Aristotle, making it more accessible.
A subtle and powerful use: the indirect commentary

Here is one of the most interesting uses of the word, and it's worth understanding because it appears often in writing and speech.

Sometimes, something that isn't literally a piece of writing or speech is described as "making a commentary." Consider the sentence: "The film's ending is a sharp commentary on how society treats the elderly." The film doesn't write an essay or give a speech. But through its story, its images, its characters, it reveals something about the world — it holds up a mirror to society and says, implicitly, look at this, consider this. That act of revealing or reflecting is called a commentary.

Similarly: "The abandoned factories stand as a silent commentary on decades of economic neglect." The factories say nothing. But their mere existence communicates something about what happened to those communities. This metaphorical use of "commentary" is very common and very powerful. It means: this thing, by its very nature, tells us something important about the world.
The difference between commentary and similar words

These distinctions will help you use the word precisely.

A review is focused specifically on evaluating quality — whether something is good or bad, worth your time or not. Commentary is broader. It can include evaluation, but it can also describe, explain, or analyze without judging quality at all.

An analysis systematically breaks something down into parts to understand how it works. Commentary is more flexible and personal — it can include analysis, but it can also include storytelling, opinion, personal reaction, and moral reflection. Analysis tends to be formal and detached; commentary tends to have more of a voice.

A narration tells you what happened. Commentary goes a step further — it also tells you what it means, why it matters, or what the narrator thinks about it.

A critique homes in on finding weaknesses or strengths in something. Commentary is wider in scope — a commentary can be entirely positive, entirely neutral, or entirely critical. "Critique" implies a more adversarial or evaluative stance, while "commentary" simply implies a sustained, thoughtful response.

Commentary is not a passing remark or a casual one-line reaction. It implies something sustained — a real engagement with a subject, with some depth. A brief comment is not really a commentary. Commentary involves thinking through something at greater length.

Commentary is also not the subject itself. This seems obvious, but it matters. The game is not the commentary on the game. The poem is not the commentary on the poem. Commentary is always secondary — it depends on a primary subject to exist.
The plural is commentaries. You would say: "She has written three commentaries on Shakespeare's tragedies." Or: "The book includes commentaries from historians, scientists, and poets."

If you had to carry one mental image of this word, carry this one: a commentary is a voice responding to something in the world. It could be a sports announcer responding to a live match, a scholar responding to an ancient text, a journalist responding to a political event, or an artist whose work silently responds to the injustices of their time. In every case, there is something out there — a subject — and the commentary wraps around it, illuminating it, interpreting it, judging it, or simply holding it up to the light so others can see it more clearly.
3079:
A commentator is a person who watches, listens to, or reads something — and then explains, describes, or gives their opinion about it to an audience.

The key idea is that a commentator does not just report what happened. They also add meaning to it. They help the audience understand what is going on, why it matters, or what to think about it.
The Two Main Types of Commentators

There are two broad ways the word is used, and understanding both will give you the full picture.

1. A live commentator (especially in sports)

This is the person you hear on TV or radio who speaks while an event is happening. Think of a cricket match, a football game, or the Olympics. The commentator narrates the action in real time — telling you what is happening on the field, who scored, what move was just made, and often adding excitement, analysis, and background information.

Their job is to be the audience's guide through the event. Without them, a viewer watching from far away might miss details, lose track of the action, or not understand certain plays. The commentator bridges that gap.

A sports commentator doesn't just say "he kicked the ball." They say "What a powerful strike from the left flank — this could be the turning point of the match!"

2. A commentator on news, politics, or social issues

This type of commentator does not describe live events. Instead, they analyze and share opinions about things happening in the world — news stories, government decisions, social trends, and so on.

You find these commentators on news channels, in newspapers, on podcasts, and online. They are sometimes called political commentators, social commentators, or media commentators.

Their job is not to be neutral like a reporter. A reporter tells you what happened. A commentator tells you what it means, why it matters, and sometimes what should be done about it. They bring perspective, expertise, and judgment.

A political commentator might appear on a news channel after an election and explain: "Here is why this result happened, what it signals about the country, and what we should expect next."

A few things define a commentator:

  • They have an audience. A commentator speaks or writes for people — viewers, readers, or listeners. Without an audience, there is no commentary.
  • They interpret, not just describe. Anyone can say "it rained heavily today." A commentator says "this is the worst flooding the region has seen in a decade, and here's why it was predictable."
  • They have some level of authority or knowledge. People trust commentators because they are seen as informed — either from experience, expertise, or careful observation.
  • They can express opinions. Unlike a neutral journalist, commentators are generally expected to share a point of view. Their commentary is colored by their analysis and judgment.

The word "commentator" appears across many domains:

  • Sports: "The cricket commentator kept the audience engaged through a slow over."
  • Politics and news: "She is a well-known political commentator who appears regularly on television."
  • Literature and academia: A scholar who writes detailed notes and explanations about a book or ancient text can also be called a commentator. (Example: "Medieval commentators wrote extensively on Aristotle's works.")
  • Social media and online spaces: Today, the word is also used loosely for people who regularly share opinions online — bloggers, YouTubers, podcasters — though this usage is more informal.

It helps to know how "commentator" differs from words that seem close to it:

  • Reporter / Journalist: Reports facts, aims to be neutral and objective. A commentator goes further by adding analysis and opinion.
  • Narrator: Describes a sequence of events (like in a film or documentary) without necessarily analyzing them. A commentator actively interprets and evaluates.
  • Analyst: Very similar to a commentator, but "analyst" often implies a more data-driven, technical, or neutral approach. A commentator can be more opinionated and expressive.
  • Critic: Focuses specifically on evaluating the quality of something (a film, a book, a performance). A commentator has a wider scope — they may analyze, explain, or evaluate, but they are not limited to judgment of quality.

A commentator is a person who observes events or issues and communicates their description, explanation, or opinion about them to an audience — whether live during a sports match, or through media when discussing news and public affairs.
